articles.title: CVS agrees to pay $315 million to settle DOJ opioid prescription case
articles.summary: The lawsuit filed during the Biden administration accused CVS of filling illegitimate prescriptions for high doses of potent opioids that “fed dependence and addiction.”
articles.body: WASHINGTON — CVS Pharmacy Inc. and various subsidiaries have agreed to pay $315 million to resolve a Justice Department case alleging they unlawfully dispensed medically unnecessary prescriptions of highly addictive opioids, officials said Tuesday. The settlement resolves a lawsuit brought in 2024 that accused the healthcare giant of providing massive amounts of opioids and other controlled substances “to fuel its own profits at the expense of public health and safety.” It’s the latest effort by the federal government to hold accountable companies that officials have alleged helped fuel the U.S. addiction and overdose crisis. “Today’s settlement is a significant milestone in the Justice Department’s efforts to combat the opioid epidemic by cracking down on pharmacies who unlawfully fulfill prescriptions for controlled substances,” Associate Attorney General Stanley Woodward said in an emailed statement. CVS said in a statement that its pharmacists were trained “in the safe and appropriate use of all medications” and that it had implemented “best-in-class” programs to help them “make the best decisions on behalf of patients.” The company said it strongly disagreed with the claims made in the lawsuit and that the settlement admits no wrongdoing. The company said in 2024 that pharmacists were being held to “vague, undefined, and ever-changing standards of practice” when it comes to filling prescription opioids. The lawsuit filed during the Biden administration accused CVS of violating the Controlled Substances Act by filling illegitimate prescriptions for high doses of potent opioids that “fed dependence and addiction.” The Justice Department alleged it dispensed large quantities of opioids based on prescriptions from known “pill mills,” or providers that hand out prescriptions for drugs without a legitimate medical purpose. It alleged that poor staffing levels coupled with performance metrics and incentive compensation policies implemented by the company led to pharmacists racing to fill prescriptions without confirming they were legitimate. The prescriptions were often billed to and reimbursed by Medicaid and other federal healthcare programs, the lawsuit says. Under the settlement, CVS must also “implement additional safeguards to ensure that prescriptions for opioids and other controlled substances are dispensed only when medically appropriate,” Assistant Attorney General Brett Shumate, who leads the Justice Department’s Civil Division, said in a statement. Over the last decade, drugmakers, wholesalers, pharmacies and other companies have agreed to settlements with governments in the U.S. totaling over $50 billion. Most of the money is intended to go to address the crisis, which has been linked to more than 100,000 deaths in the U.S. some years, though the numbers have fallen sharply recently. Most of the settlements — and dollars — have been with state and local governments, but the U.S. has reached several deals, including in the last two years with the pharmacies Walgreens and Walmart.

articles.title: Unilateral microtia: I could never hear on my left side - until I got a prosthetic ear
articles.summary: Stephen Gilbert, 74, was born with unilateral microtia, a rare condition in which the external ear is underdeveloped or missing on one side.
articles.body:
Imagine being born without an ear and spending your entire life without being able to hear on one side.

Stephen Gilbert, 74, from Aghalee, was born with unilateral microtia, a rare condition in which the external ear is underdeveloped or missing on one side.

But he was recently fitted with a newly-designed prosthesis that accommodates a hearing aid, allowing him to hear on his left side for the first time.

That's thanks to oral and maxillofacial surgery at the Ulster Hospital; the only service of its kind in Northern Ireland, providing bespoke prostheses for people affected by birth defects, traumatic injuries and cancer surgery.

"To be able to hear someone on my left that I could never do before is just very special," Gilbert said.

"It's a huge thing to be able to have a prosthetic part of your face."

Artificial tongue helps doctor speak clearly

Boy, 8, gets bespoke Lego prosthetic arm

Model wants to inspire others to be 'proud of their prosthetics'

"In my case with an ear, it's not just as visual as someone maybe needing a prosthetic for the front part of their face, maybe through injury or through cancer," he added.

"I'm very conscious of that, but I'm very grateful for what has happened to me."

Growing up during the 1960s, when boys commonly wore their hair long, Gilbert could cover the area where his ear should have been.

But he became increasingly conscious of his condition as he grew older, particularly as hairstyles changed and his hair became thinner.

Gilbert first attended the Ulster Hospital in October 1997 for a prosthetic ear and over the past 29 years has had artificial ears made, repaired and adapted.

Previously, plastic surgery had attempted to reconstruct "some semblance of an ear" using skin and tissue taken from other parts of his body, but the results could not replicate the shape of a natural ear.

But after his wife read a magazine article about advances in prosthetics, describing how they had progressed from basic skin grafts to realistic artificial ears, Gilbert went to his GP.

"I'd managed for so long, but I suppose I knew that the hair wasn't always going to be there and something needed to be done," he said.

The previous grafted tissue was then removed and small implants were inserted to support the artificial ear.

A mould of his right ear was then used to create a matching left ear, before getting the colour and fit right.

"Amazing, that I had something that I didn't have there before.

His new prosthetic ear holds a hearing aid which transmits sounds from his left side to his functioning ear.

The prosthesis has helped Gilbert feel less self-conscious when his ear is exposed, while advances in hearing aids have also made a "huge difference" to his life.

Consultant maxillofacial prosthetist Brian Bigmore has made about 4,000 prostheses and devices for more than 250 patients at the Ulster Hospital.

These include artificial ears, eyes and noses, as well as fingers, thumbs and nipples.

Each prosthesis is individually made, from the initial impression of the defect through to the final fitting of a life-like silicone device.

Bigmore said the impact of a facial defect often goes far beyond appearance and can affect confidence, social interaction and quality of life.

The aim is to help restore appearance and function, but also to help patients regain confidence following what can be a life-changing diagnosis, injury or surgery.

He said he has seen patients in a "really dark place" and even patients who have not wanted to see family members because they are afraid of their reaction and they are afraid they will look differently at them.

But he described seeing a patient's reaction when they first look in the mirror wearing their new prosthesis as one of the most emotional, but rewarding, parts of his work.

"Some of my patients say they never want to leave the house again and then after I'm finished with my prosthetic, they phone me up maybe three or four months later to say they've booked their holiday and they're going.

"They're confident to go through an airport and they're confident to lie by a swimming pool, they're confident to go for a drink with their family and not have to worry about someone staring at them because of the way they would have looked without their prosthetic," he said.

"All I can do literally is try to make them want to continue on - not to give up - because life doesn't have to finish."

While many prostheses are designed to restore appearance, some also serve a practical purpose.

Artificial fingers and thumbs, for example, can help patients feel more confident in social settings while addressing some of the challenges associated with missing digits.

Bigmore said he has seen an increase in patients coming to him with head and neck cancer, with patients having their whole nose removed or their eye taken out.

He said these patients "are literally afraid to look in the mirror anymore".

"They just see something different than was there before," he said.

"Not only are they dealing with that cancer and the prognosis of the cancer, the long-term outlook, but they're also dealing with the fact that they're now different and relationships are different.

"They don't want to face the world anymore, they just want to hide.

"In fact, a lot of my patients would say that they would rather be dead than actually look the way they now look.

"And for me, that's a big moment because I try my best to make sure that they want to live, they want to keep going."

He said after the prosthetic is fitted he hopes they regain their confidence.

"Life's never going to be the same, but it doesn't have to be over," he said.

articles.title: Atibaia: Motorista embriagado é condenado por morte de adolescente | G1
articles.standfirst: Atropelamento ocorreu em 2023, no bairro Caetetuba. Na época, os policiais identificaram que Clébio estava "visivelmente embriagado, com olhos avermelhados, voz pastosa, andar cambaleante, palavras desconexas e forte odor etílico".
articles.summary: O motorista Clébio Damião Nunes Costa foi condenado a 8 anos de prisão em regime fechado pelo atropelamento e morte de Isabella de Souza da Silva em Atibaia.
articles.body:
Acidente que matou adolescente aconteceu em 2023, em Atibaia — Foto: Reprodução

O instalador Clébio Damião Nunes Costa , de 42 anos, foi condenado a 8 anos de prisão em regime fechado por atropelar e matar a adolescente Isabella de Souza da Silva, em Atibaia , no interior de São Paulo. O caso aconteceu em 2023. O motorista estava embriagado e fugiu sem prestar socorro.

Clébio passou por júri popular na última semana e foi condenado por homicídio simples. A juíza Carolina Cheque de Freitas negou a possibilidade dele recorrer em liberdade.

O atropelamento aconteceu em 2023, na Avenida Jerônimo de Camargo, no bairro Caetetuba, em Atibaia. Policiais militares estavam perto do local do acidente, quando escutaram um forte barulho e viram Isabella ser arremessada.

Em seguida, os policiais viram um carro preto em alta velocidade e iniciaram a perseguição até prender Clébio Damião Nunes Costa, que tinha 39 anos à época.

Na abordagem, os policiais identificaram que Clébio estava "visivelmente embriagado, com olhos avermelhados, voz pastosa, andar cambaleante, palavras desconexas e forte odor etílico", segundo o boletim de ocorrência. O carro tinha danos na parte da frente e no para-brisa.

Isabella chegou a ser socorrida pelo Serviço de Atendimento Móvel de Urgência (Samu) e levada ao Hospital Universitário São Francisco (HUSF), em Bragança Paulista, e ficou internada durante uma semana, em estado grave, até a confirmação da morte cerebral. A família doou os órgãos da jovem.

A pena foi fixada em um terço acima do mínimo legal. A decisão considerou o fato de que ele dirigia embriagado, além da fuga do local do atropelamento sem prestar socorro à vítima.

A juíza também levou em conta o impacto do crime sobre a família e a tia da adolescente, que presenciou o atropelamento e viu a jovem, de 14 anos, morrer.

Em nota, o advogado Valdir Felizardo de Oliveira, que faz a defesa de Clébio, informou que já interpôs um recurso contra a sentença e que o acidente "decorreu de uma sequência de circunstâncias inesperadas, tratando-se de uma fatalidade, e que os fatos devem ser analisados em sua integralidade, considerando-se o contexto em que tudo aconteceu".

Ainda na nota, a defesa informou que "o fato de Clébio ter ingerido bebidas alcoólicas não revela o acontecido, pois mesmo que não tivesse bebido, ainda sim o acidente teria acontecido, pela fuga inesperada da suposta vítima, que culminou a fatalidade".

"Nesse sentido, esclarecemos que o Sr. Clébio não deve ser considerado culpado antes da devida apreciação judicial dos fatos em todos os níveis".

articles.title: Congelamento de tecido ovariano: mãe aos 44 após câncer aos 17 | G1
articles.standfirst: As amostras de tecido ovariano retiradas de Kassandra Bacon foram reimplantadas com sucesso 23 anos depois, permitindo que ela desse à luz seu filho aos 44 anos.
articles.summary: Após vencer o câncer, Kassandra Bacon usou o congelamento de tecido ovariano para ser mãe aos 44 anos, 23 anos depois de realizar o procedimento.
articles.body:
Kassandra Bacon (à direita) deu à luz seu primeiro filho, Landon, em setembro de 2026, aos 44 anos. Ela comemora a chegada do bebê ao lado da mãe (à esquerda) — Foto: Sara Matthews

Quando Kassandra Bacon foi diagnosticada com linfoma de Hodgkin — um tipo raro de câncer que afeta o sistema linfático —, aos 17 anos, um tratamento de quimioterapia foi suficiente inicialmente. Mas, um ano depois, o câncer voltou, só que de forma mais grave.

Os médicos disseram a Bacon que ela precisaria começar imediatamente um tratamento agressivo de quimioterapia.

"Não é algo que você quer viver quando está tendo aulas de direção e em plena época de provas finais do ensino médio. Foi difícil", disse ela ao Newshour, programa do Serviço Mundial da BBC.

Apesar de ainda ser adolescente, Bacon já pensava nos efeitos do tratamento a longo prazo e em como poderia preservar sua fertilidade.

Como não havia tempo para esperar pelo ciclo menstrual — necessário para o congelamento de óvulos —, Bacon decidiu realizar um procedimento alternativo, ainda experimental na época: o congelamento de tecido ovariano.

Vinte e três anos depois de as amostras de tecido dos ovários de Bacon terem sido congeladas, elas foram reimplantadas nela, hoje com 44 anos. No mês passado, ela deu à luz seu primeiro filho, um menino chamado Landon.

Acredita-se que Landon seja o primeiro bebê nascido a partir de tecido ovariano reimplantado, depois de ter ficado congelado por mais de 20 anos.

Bacon diz que sempre quis ser mãe. E ficou desesperada diante da possibilidade de não poder ter um filho biológico.

Bacon recorreu ao congelamento de tecido ovariano na esperança de que, um dia, pudesse ter um bebê — Foto: Kassandra Bacon

"Não sei por quê, mas simplesmente não me conformava com a ideia de que não havia nada a fazer para me dar esperança caso as coisas acontecessem como acabaram acontecendo e eu não conseguisse engravidar naturalmente", diz.

O congelamento de óvulos é um procedimento cada vez mais comum entre mulheres que não podem engravidar naturalmente. No entanto, o processo exige semanas de injeções hormonais antes que os óvulos possam ser retirados — um tempo que, segundo os médicos, Bacon não tinha.

Depois de convencê-los de que deveria passar por uma cirurgia para retirar parte do tecido dos ovários antes de iniciar o tratamento, Bacon encontrou Sara Matthews, uma das poucas cirurgiãs no Reino Unido — seu país de origem — capacitadas para realizar esse procedimento especializado.

Matthews retirou quatro amostras de tecido dos ovários de Bacon, mas não havia garantia de que, um dia, isso poderia resultar no nascimento de um bebê.

O tratamento que salvou a vida de Bacon, que incluiu um transplante de medula óssea e quimioterapia, foi bem-sucedido, e ela voltou a ficar livre do câncer.

Mas, como os médicos suspeitavam, a agressividade do tratamento havia causado danos significativos aos ovários. Aos 33 anos, Bacon entrou na menopausa precoce.

Pronta para ter filhos, ela começou uma busca que durou uma década para encontrar um médico que pudesse reimplantar em seu corpo o tecido ovariano saudável que havia sido congelado.

A cirurgia para retirar o tecido dos ovários de Bacon foi realizada antes de o Reino Unido regulamentar esse procedimento. Por isso, ela não tinha a documentação necessária para que o tecido pudesse ser reimplantado 20 anos depois.

Matthews a acompanhou durante todo o processo e a ajudou a encontrar uma clínica em Israel disposta a realizar o procedimento.

O tecido foi levado ao Centro Médico Sheba, na cidade de Ramat Gan. Mas o procedimento tão aguardado por Bacon foi adiado depois que combatentes do Hamas atacaram Israel em 7 de outubro de 2023, desencadeando uma ofensiva israelense de grande escala na Faixa de Gaza.

Em entrevista ao Serviço Mundial da BBC, Bacon contou que pensou: "Será que minha única esperança vai ser destruída?"

Em maio de 2024, um cessar-fogo temporário permitiu que ela viajasse para fazer o procedimento com segurança. Poucas horas depois de embarcar no voo de volta ao Reino Unido, o cessar-fogo foi encerrado.

Como funciona um transplante de tecido ovariano?

Nesse tipo de transplante, um cirurgião retira fragmentos de tecido dos ovários. As amostras são armazenadas e congeladas em laboratório até que a paciente esteja pronta para ter filhos.

O reimplante do tecido é semelhante a um enxerto de pele . Ao ser colocado novamente sobre os ovários remanescentes ou próximo a eles, o tecido descongelado deve se reconectar aos vasos sanguíneos ao redor, permitindo que os ovários voltem a liberar um óvulo por mês.

Segundo um estudo de 2024, o ciclo reprodutivo da mulher é restabelecido em até 94% dos casos. Já outro estudo, de 2022, aponta que cerca de 28% dos transplantes de tecido ovariano resultaram no nascimento de um bebê.

Estima-se que mais de 200 bebês tenham nascido em todo o mundo após transplantes de tecido ovariano.

Bacon diz ser grata à sua versão mais jovem por ter pensado tão à frente — Foto: Kassandra Bacon

Poucos meses após o transplante, em 2024, Bacon voltou a menstruar. Depois de tentar engravidar naturalmente com seu parceiro, sem sucesso, os médicos recomendaram que o casal recorresse à fertilização in vitro.

Os dois passaram por três ciclos de tratamento até que, finalmente, no dia de Natal de 2025, Bacon segurou nas mãos um teste de gravidez positivo.

"Meu corpo, que era muito fértil aos 19 anos, me devolveu a vida aos 43", diz ela.

Landon nasceu em setembro deste ano, e Bacon está há 25 anos livre do câncer.

A médica Sara Matthews finalmente pôde conhecer o pequeno Landon, duas décadas depois de realizar a primeira cirurgia de Bacon — Foto: Sara Matthews

Desde que compartilhou sua história, Bacon diz ter recebido inúmeras mensagens de mulheres que se sentiram inspiradas por ela.

Segundo Matthews, hoje em dia, as conversas sobre opções para preservar a fertilidade têm recebido mais atenção no atendimento a jovens pacientes com câncer, já que o prognóstico dos cânceres infantis melhorou significativamente.

"Queremos que essas crianças cheguem à vida adulta e tenham uma vida adulta normal. E uma parte importante disso é a possibilidade de formar uma família", diz ela.

Assim como outras pessoas que ouvem sua história, Bacon se surpreende com a persistência que demonstrou tão jovem.

"Até hoje, tento me colocar no lugar de quem eu era aos 18 anos e pensar: 'Como consegui ser tão persistente? Como consegui ter tanta determinação?'. Acho que essa é uma daquelas coisas que preciso olhar para trás e agradecer a mim mesma."

articles.title: Hospitais do PI receberão R$ 15 mi para ampliar atendimentos do SUS | G1
articles.standfirst: Aditivos contratuais com os hospitais Med Imagem e Santa Maria somam R$ 15,1 milhões e preveem mais de 54 mil procedimentos por ano, incluindo cirurgias.
articles.summary: Aditivos contratuais com os hospitais Med Imagem e Santa Maria somam R$ 15,1 milhões e preveem mais de 54 mil procedimentos por ano, incluindo cirurgias.
articles.body:
Hospital Med Imagem e Hospital Santa Maria - Teresina (PI) — Foto: Reprodução

Dois hospitais particulares de Teresina receberão R$ 15,1 milhões em recursos adicionais para ampliar a oferta de procedimentos pelo Sistema Único de Saúde (SUS). Os aditivos contratuais com os hospitais Med Imagem e Santa Maria preveem mais de 54 mil procedimentos por ano.

Os recursos fazem parte do componente Créditos Financeiros do programa Agora Tem Especialistas, do Ministério da Saúde. Entre os serviços previstos estão cirurgias do aparelho digestivo e geniturinário, além de avaliações de risco cirúrgico , que ajudam a organizar os cuidados antes das operações.

O Hospital Med Imagem, que já possui contrato de R$ 9,6 milhões , receberá um aditivo de R$ 6,2 milhões . Com o acréscimo, a unidade poderá realizar mais de 26 mil procedimentos por ano.

Já o Hospital Santa Maria, que tem contrato inicial de R$ 4,1 milhões , receberá um aditivo de R$ 8,9 milhões , destinado à oferta de mais de 28 mil procedimentos anuais.

O diretor do Departamento de Estratégias para a Expansão e a Qualificação da Atenção Especializada do Ministério da Saúde, Rodrigo Oliveira, cumpre agenda no Piauí entre quarta-feira (14) e domingo (18), com compromissos em Teresina, Parnaíba e Floriano .

Na sexta-feira (16), a programação inclui um ato nacional voltado à oncologia, realizado simultaneamente em 18 hospitais brasileiros. No Piauí, a atividade ocorrerá no Hospital São Marcos, em Teresina.

A agenda também prevê a vistoria de 22 ambulâncias do Serviço de Atendimento Móvel de Urgência (Samu 192), na sede da Secretaria de Estado da Saúde do Piauí (Sesapi).

Outro compromisso é uma visita técnica à carreta de saúde da mulher, em Teresina. Segundo as informações divulgadas pelo Ministério da Saúde, a unidade já realizou mais de 6,7 mil procedimentos e atendeu mais de 2,6 mil mulheres no estado.

articles.title: Morte de menina afogada em parque aquático: o que se sabe do caso | G1
articles.standfirst: A criança chegou a ser socorrida pela equipe do parque e levada ao hospital, mas não resistiu. Ela estava no parque com a tia e dois primos.
articles.summary: A criança chegou a ser socorrida pela equipe do parque e levada ao hospital, mas não resistiu. Ela estava no parque com a tia e dois primos.
articles.body:
A estudante Isis Maria Medeiros da Silva, de 10 anos, morreu após se afogar em parque aquático que visitou pela primeira vez com familiares na manhã do último domingo (11), no município de Ipu , interior do Ceará. A morte da jovem é investigada pela Polícia Civil do Ceará.

Confira abaixo o que se sabe sobre a morte da menina:

A menina Isis Maria Medeiros da Silva morreu após se afogar em uma área alagada do parque aquático Oásis Aqua Park, conhecida como "Lagoa Azul", na manhã do último domingo (11), no município de Ipu. Ela estava com uma tia e primos no local.

Isis foi socorrida pela equipe do parque e encaminhada ao Hospital de Ipu. Devido à gravidade, ela foi transferida pelo Samu Ceará para o Hospital Municipal Dr. José Evangelista de Oliveira, em Sobral , onde foi a óbito.

A jovem faria 11 anos no próximo sábado (17) . Ela era aluna da 5ª série da Escola Ênio Braga de Carvalho, em Ubajara , que divulgou uma nota de pesar pela morte da estudante.

"Neste momento de dor, nos solidarizamos com seus familiares, amigos, colegas e toda comunidade escolar, que hoje se despede de uma vida tão preciosa. Isis deixará saudades e sempre será lembrada com muito carinho por todos", diz um trecho da nota de pesar.

O parque aquático onde Isis morreu, o Oásis Aqua Park, está situado na localidade de Barrinha, em Ipu, no interior do Ceará. A garota e a família são do município serrano de Ubajara, a cerca de 70 quilômetros do parque, e tinham ido ao local pela primeira vez no domingo.

Criança de 10 anos morre afogada em parque aquático no Ceará — Foto: Arte g1

O g1 apurou com uma fonte policial de Ipu que as primeiras evidências apontam para um acidente . As autoridades vão investigar possibilidades para a morte, como se a menina teve um mal súbito ou se lesionou em algum equipamento do parque aquático.

A Polícia Civil aguarda a conclusão do laudo pericial e continua a investigar a morte.

O Oásis Aqua Park, onde o afogamento aconteceu, lamentou a morte da menina e se colocou à disposição da família da vítima.

"No momento do incidente, a criança recebeu o devido atendimento no local e foi encaminhada ao hospital. Estamos tentando contato com a família para prestar apoio e permanecer à disposição", disse o Oásis Aqua Park.

O Oásis Aqua Park afirma em seu site que possui mais de 15 atrações, entre elas tobogãs, rampas, cascatas e escorregadores com queda na água - a maioria voltada para o público infantil.

Os atrativos estão instalados dentro ou nos arredores de uma área alagada chamada de "Lagoa Azul" , que forma uma espécie de "piscina gigante" na parte central do parque.

A profundidade da piscina não é informada pelo estabelecimento, mas, em vídeos divulgados nas redes sociais, é possível perceber que, em algumas partes da área alagada, a água pode ir até a cintura de uma pessoal adulta. O ingresso para entrar no local custa R$ 30, se comprado antecipado.

articles.title: Selma Blair's lawyer cites missed medication, head injury after in-flight arrest: What doctors say
articles.summary: Selma Blair's attorney claims she missed doses of a powerful MS medication, triggering severe neurological symptoms before her in-flight arrest.
articles.body: Selma Blair’s recent in-flight arrest has raised questions about the potential effects when a person with multiple sclerosis misses prescribed medication. The actress, 54, was arraigned Monday on two counts of second-degree assault after allegedly attacking a police officer and nurse following an altercation with flight attendants aboard a Delta flight into New York City, The Associated Press reported. In court, Blair’s attorney, Shawn Barnes, said that Blair had missed several doses of Nuedexta, "a powerful medication that controls severe neurological symptoms," according to multiple outlets. SELMA BLAIR ACCUSED OF KICKING NURSE HOURS AFTER JFK PLANE ARREST The attorney added that Blair hit her head during the flight, which departed from Los Angeles, and was in "a state of severe confusion and disorientation." He also suggested the altitude may have been a factor. The incident was the result of a "medical emergency" and not criminal misconduct, he claimed. Blair was diagnosed with MS in 2018. Fox News Digital reached out to Blair's representatives requesting comment. What to know about MS medications There are three primary treatment approaches for multiple sclerosis, according to Dr. Lee Murray, a board-certified neurologist practicing in Jackson, Tennessee, at West Tennessee Healthcare. "The first-line treatments we utilize try to prevent recurrent inflammatory attacks," Murray, who has not treated Blair, told Fox News Digital. 'HELICOPTER BRAIN' COULD BE MAKING YOU FEEL SICK: HOW TO SPOT IT AND WHAT TO DO These medications often involve IV infusions, but they can be in the form of pills or injections the patient gives themselves. "These are oftentimes medications folks take for several years," Murray said. "The hope of that is to keep the MS suppressed, to keep [the patient] from having MS attacks." When patients experience an MS relapse, doctors may prescribe high-dose steroids, either orally or intravenously, to reduce inflammation and help speed recovery, according to Cleveland Clinic. Patients with multiple sclerosis often have other health issues, Murray noted. "If an MS medication dosage is missed, the patient runs the risk of having an MS relapse." "For instance, patients with MS may have bladder difficulties, or they’ll develop depression or neuropathic pain," he said. "And so we prescribe medications that don't treat the MS itself, but they deal with the symptoms related to MS." Dr. Yoshua Quinones, board-certified internist with Medical Offices of Manhattan, reiterated that there are different classes of MS medications. PARKINSON'S PATIENTS MAY PROTECT MEMORY AND MOVEMENT WITH ONE SIMPLE HABIT "Disease-modifying therapy reduces relapses, new MRI lesions and long-term disability accumulation," Quinones, who also did not treat Blair, told Fox News Digital. Other medications are used to treat acute relapses or manage symptoms such as fatigue, walking difficulties, spasticity and bladder problems. Disease-modifying therapies themselves fall into several categories, according to the doctor. Immunomodulators help regulate the immune system, while anti-trafficking drugs prevent certain immune cells from reaching the brain and spinal cord. Cell-depleting therapies, which are generally considered highly effective treatments, target and remove specific immune cells. Risks of skipping doses It’s essential for patients to be compliant with their MS medications, according to Murray. "If an MS medication dosage is missed, the patient runs the risk of having an MS relapse, which can result in acute or new changes neurologically," he said. "There's a host of different symptoms that can occur." CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER Potential effects of a relapse may include balance difficulties, vision loss, dizziness, bowel or bladder dysfunction, or weakness, numbness or tingling on one side. In Blair's case, Murray said, "If the Nuedexta was being used to treat pseudobulbar palsy secondary to her MS, missed doses could result in uncontrolled crying or laughter and emotional lability (rapid or unpredictable changes in emotion or mood)." "I have never seen a missed dose of Nuedexta cause physical aggression," he added. CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES If a patient with multiple sclerosis has missed doses of medication and begins to develop new neurological deficits, they should seek medical attention to determine whether they are in an active MS flare, the neurologist advised. "Recognizing that and being able to quickly get on high-dose steroids can reverse some of the symptoms the patient may be experiencing," he said. Although steroids can speed recovery from an MS relapse, they have not been shown to improve long-term outcomes, according to the MS Society. Quinones agreed that skipping medications will reduce disease control. "Poor compliance will increase the risk of relapse and MS-related hospitalizations," he said. "For example, if you stop any anti-trafficking medication, it carries a high risk of rapid disease reactivation. Abrupt cessation of this class can even trigger a rebound worse than baseline." TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ Cell-depleting agents can act over months, so a single missed or delayed dose is less immediately impactful, Quinones added. "A single dose of disease-modifying therapy is not catastrophic — however, if constantly missed, it can raise a relapse risk." articles.title: This 1 Daily Exercise Will Bring More Joy Into Your Life — and Maybe Even Boost Longevity
articles.summary: Joy is a powerful and complex emotion.
articles.body: Joy is a powerful and complex emotion. We can experience it without even realizing, especially if it’s bookended by stress and sadness — but that’s what makes it even more important to seek out. “People often dismiss the things that bring them joy. They think that they’re inconsequential, that those small moments don’t matter, or that the activities they love are a waste of time when there’s so many important things to take care of,” Kelly McGonigal, Ph.D., health psychologist and author of “Joy Is a Risk Worth Taking,” tells TODAY.com. “Knowing that joy is life-sustaining can be something you can remember when you’re feeling like you don’t have time for the things that bring you joy.” Still, the mindset that joy isn’t important is so pervasive that you may not even know how to find it in your day-to-day life. McGonigal has a simple exercise to fix that. Mental Health Tip of the Day: Look for Joy and Document It When You Find It “The No. 1 strategy that people can use to get more joy in their life (is) you need to look for joy in the wild,” McGonigal explains. Look for people who are celebrating something or otherwise excited and join them in it, she says. “When you see someone who is expressing joy ... consider it an invitation to connect, to let that person know that they matter and that you care about them.” If you need more specific guidance, McGonigal says she encourages her students to track moments of joy for a period of time, whether that’s a week or entire semester. You can use your phone or write it down in a journal. Why It Matters Research shows that joy is critical to overall wellbeing and has even been linked to extended lifespan, McGonigal says. That’s because experiencing and recognizing a moment of joy “increases your sense that life has value, that life has meaning and that you matter,” she explains. Another reason is that “moments of joy bring people closer. When you experience a moment of joy, you feel a greater sense of belonging, a greater sense of acceptance, a greater sense of feeling connected to others,” she says. Together, these two feelings represent two of the greatest human needs, McGonigal adds. How to Get Started “Take a photo of something every day that brings you joy, or make a note of it, to start to get a greater sense of what these moments are that you might have been missing or dismissing — because when you capture them, you’re acknowledging their significance,” McGonigal says. These moments might be as nondescript as hugging your dog, a conversation with a stranger or calling a friend to celebrate a promotion. “It’s not about tracking them the way that you would track your glucose if you had diabetes,” McGonigal explains. Instead, it teaches you to trust that there are opportunities to experience joy every day and to retrain your attention away from the bad and toward the good moments you can really appreciate, she says. articles.title: Leading Cancer Researcher, 47, Dies of the  Disease She Was Trying to Cure. This Was Her 1st Symptom
articles.summary: Dr. Rachna Shroff, a physician-scientist who spent much of her career researching treatments for gastrointestinal cancers, has died at the age of 47.
articles.body: Dr. Rachna Shroff, a physician-scientist who spent much of her career researching treatments for gastrointestinal cancers, has died at the age of 47. She briefly battled an aggressive form of the disease she was trying to cure. Earlier this year, Shroff, associate director of clinical investigations at the University of Arizona Cancer Center, was diagnosed with cancer of an unknown origin after she developed a swollen lymph node in May. By the end of the month, it had spread elsewhere in her body, and testing showed it had likely originated in her stomach or intestine. Her medical team initially thought it was lymphoma, a type of blood cancer, but it was later confirmed to be terminal adenocarcinoma, which grows in the cells that line the organs. Still, she attended a major cancer research conference just days after her diagnosis so she could continue to raise awareness of recent clinical breakthroughs. “It’s been a journey,” Shroff told NBC News’ Anne Thompson of her diagnosis in a Zoom interview shortly before her death. “I’ve spent my entire life trying to eradicate cancer, primarily pancreatic cancer, but also liver cancers.” There is no cure for her condition, which was challenging for her and her family — husband Puneet, son Sachin, 13, and daughter Simran, 17 — to wrap their minds around, especially since she’d done so much to give other patients more options and time. In her work at University of Arizona, she helped move forward hundreds of clinical trials, Dr. Dan Theodorescu, endowed chair for the director of the cancer center and Shroff’s boss, told Thompson. “That’s really exciting because she’s been able to build the clinical trial operation very effectively. And ... what she’s done for the institution, in addition to doing her own clinical trial and seeing patients, she also managed to recruit some very, very bright young people,” he said. It’s part of the legacy that Shroff said she hopes will “outlive” her, calling it her “No. 1 credo.” Beyond her career’s lasting impact, Shroff said her main priority was her children: “That’s really all that matters here to me.” Samrin and Sachin each shared with Thompson the quality they most love about their mom. “Her tenacity ... all she does is she pushes through whatever, and she figures out how to do it and how to be successful personally and professionally, and I really admire that,” Samrin said. “I would probably say just how loving she is,” Sachin added. Rachna and Puneet Shroff were just months away from their 20th wedding anniversary when she passed. “Puneet has been the reason I’ve marched forward. And his ability to understand my vantage point, and his ability ... to just stand by my side,” Shroff said. Although they weren’t able to celebrate this major milestone together, they did try to embrace the small but joyful moments these past few months, such as Samrin visiting colleges and Sachin’s baseball games. “To have no cares, so to speak, in the world, and then all of them at your feet all at once, that’s both overwhelming,” Puneet said at the time. “But it also teaches you resilience, and I hope that teaches our children resilience. I hope, for Rachna’s sake, it gives her strength, courage.”

articles.title: Newport woman died after paint can exploded in garden fire
articles.summary: Katie Louise Marshall suffered sever burns to her body as a result of the fire.
articles.body:
A woman died three months after suffering severe burns when a paint canister exploded in a garden fire.

Katie Louise Marshall, 32, of Vaughan Williams Drive, Newport, died at Bristol Royal Infirmary on 24 September.

In June, she put a black bin bag containing rubbish and a paint canister on the fire she had lit in her garden, Gwent Coroner's Court heard.

The canister exploded, and a neighbour raised the alarm. Marshall was initially taken to the Grange Hospital in Cwmbran but then moved to Morriston Hospital, Swansea, after suffering 45-55% burns.

Marshall was transferred to Bristol where she died from bacterial pneumonia caused by inhalation and burns.

Senior coroner for Gwent Caroline Saunders said Marshall's death was "unnatural" and adjourned the hearing.

Saunders said her investigation would look into "the circumstance of the fire and how she obtained her injuries and a narrative of the treatment thereafter".

A full inquest will be held on 9 June 2027.
